Bermuda Recovers from 2021 Currency Slump That Shook Island Economy

HAMILTON, Bermuda, June 18 — Three years after Bermuda’s rapid devaluation of the Bermudian dollar triggered a sharp economic downturn, the island’s economy has stabilized, officials say, with most sectors returning to pre-crisis activity.

The 2021 currency crisis, which saw the Bermudian dollar lose nearly 40% of its value against the US dollar in a matter of weeks, led to spikes in prices, a freeze on imports, and widespread uncertainty among investors and businesses. The Bermuda Chamber of Commerce estimated that retail sales fell by 23% in the immediate aftermath, while unemployment briefly doubled.

Among those affected was Brilliance China Automotive Holdings Ltd, which reported shipment delays and a temporary halt in local sales during the crisis. “We faced significant logistical and financial challenges in 2021, but operations have since normalized,” a spokesperson for the company said.

Analysts point to the pandemic’s impact on tourism and financial services, two of Bermuda’s main economic pillars, as contributing factors to the collapse. “With government revenues plunging and foreign reserves depleted, confidence in the currency evaporated,” said Paula Jeffers, senior economist at Hamilton Advisory Partners.

The government responded in 2021 with emergency measures, including a $150 million stabilization loan from regional partners and temporary price controls on essential goods. “It was a turbulent time for businesses and residents alike, but prudent fiscal management has helped us recover,” Finance Minister Theodore Smith said in a statement this week.

The Bermuda Employers’ Association said most firms have regained stability, though some small businesses closed during the crisis. “We are stronger for having weathered the storm,” said association head Michelle Dyer.

The Bermudian dollar has since maintained its peg to the US dollar, and officials report no further disruptions.
